steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Overview
  - coverage: The New York Times, Newsweek, Wired, The Economist
  - critics incl. Cosma Shalizi, Scott Aaronson: fatal flaw - simple systems like cellular automata not complex enough for evolved systems; Wolfram ignored research categorizing complexity
  - critics accept universal computation result but see it as minor; dispute paradigm shift
  - others: valuable insights, refreshing ideas
  - Wolfram answered critics in blog posts
## Scientific philosophy
- tenet: simpler system -> more likely to recur in more complicated contexts
- so exploring space of simple programs -> base of reusable knowledge
- objection: only some of all possible parameters occur in universe; e.g. most permutations of an equation's symbols meaningless
- criticized for claiming simple systems representative of all systems
## Methodology
- doesn't follow established scientific methodology
  - no rigorous mathematical definitions; no theorem proving
  - formulas in Mathematica, not standard notation
- heavily visual; pictures lack formal meaning
- ignores modern complexity research, esp. rigorous mathematical work
- misrepresents chaos theory
## Utility
- no specific results immediately applicable to ongoing research
- simple programs little connection to physical universe -> limited value
- Steven Weinberg: no real-world system satisfactorily explained by Wolfram's methods
- Steven G. Krantz: [quote: leopard spots - cooking up an automaton doesn't mean understanding mechanism/function]
## PCE
- vague, unmathematical, no directly verifiable predictions
- contrary to spirit of mathematical logic / computational complexity theory (fine-grained distinctions); conflates kinds of universality
- Ray Kurzweil: ignores hardware vs software distinction - equivalent computers != equivalent programs
- others: just a rechristening of Church–Turing thesis
## Fundamental theory (Chapter 9)
- speculations on fundamental physics: vague, obsolete
- Scott Aaronson (Prof. CS, University of Texas Austin): can't be compatible with both special relativity and Bell's theorem violations -> can't explain Bell tests
- Edward Fredkin, Konrad Zuse pioneered computable universe; the former: line in his book on world maybe like a cellular automaton; later developed by Fredkin with toy model Salt
  - claim NKS takes these as its own; but Wolfram's model = rewriting network, not CA; Wolfram: CA can't handle relativistic features like no absolute time frame
- Jürgen Schmidhuber: his Turing-machine-computable physics work taken without attribution (enumerating Turing-computable universes)
- Weinberg 2002 review (Nobel laureate, particle physicist): [quote: lapsed particle physicist ... carpenter, moon, wood]
## Natural selection
- Wolfram: natural selection not fundamental cause of biological complexity
- Chris Lavers (journalist): Wolfram doesn't understand evolution
## Originality
- not original/important enough for title and claims
- authoritative presentation suggests everything is Wolfram's own
- rule 110 Turing completeness not proven by Wolfram; credited to research assistant Matthew Cook

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Newspapers and magazines covered A New Kind of Science, including articles in The New York Times, Newsweek, Wired, and The Economist. Some scientists criticized the book, including Cosma Shalizi and Scott Aaronson. They saw a fatal flaw in it, which is that simple systems like cellular automata are not complex enough to describe how complex evolved systems are, and they said Wolfram ignored the research that categorizes the complexity of systems. The critics accept Wolfram's result that shows universal computation, but they think it is minor and they dispute his claim that it is a paradigm shift. Other people thought the work had valuable insights and refreshing ideas. Wolfram answered his critics in a series of blog posts.

## Scientific philosophy

One tenet of NKS is that the simpler a system is, the more likely it is that a version of it will recur in many more complicated contexts. So NKS argues that if you explore the space of simple programs systematically you will get a base of knowledge that can be reused. But a lot of scientists believe that out of all possible parameters only some actually occur in the universe. For example, out of all the possible permutations of the symbols that make up an equation, most will be basically meaningless. NKS has also been criticized for saying that the behavior of simple systems is somehow representative of all systems.

## Methodology

A common criticism is that NKS does not follow the established scientific methodology. For example, NKS does not give rigorous mathematical definitions and it does not try to prove theorems, and most of the formulas and equations are written in Mathematica and not in standard notation. In the same way NKS has been criticized for being very visual, with a lot of the information given in pictures that don't have formal meaning. It was also criticized for not using modern research in the field of complexity, especially work on complexity from a rigorous mathematical perspective. It was also criticized for misrepresenting chaos theory.

## Utility

NKS has been criticized for not giving specific results that can be applied right away to ongoing scientific research. There is also criticism, implicit and explicit, that studying simple programs has little connection to the physical universe and so it is of limited value. Steven Weinberg pointed out that no real-world system has been satisfactorily explained with Wolfram's methods. The mathematician Steven G. Krantz wrote, "Just because Wolfram can cook up a cellular automaton that seems to produce the spot pattern on a leopard, may we safely conclude that he understands the mechanism by which the spots are produced on the leopard, or why the spots are there, or what function (evolutionary or mating or camouflage or other) they perform?"

## Principle of computational equivalence (PCE)

- vague, unmathematical, no directly verifiable predictions
- contrary to spirit of mathematical logic / computational complexity theory (fine-grained distinctions); conflates kinds of universality
- Ray Kurzweil: ignores hardware vs software - equivalent computers != equivalent programs
- others: just a rechristening of Church–Turing thesis

## The fundamental theory (NKS Chapter 9)

- speculations on fundamental physics: vague, obsolete
- Scott Aaronson (Prof. CS, University of Texas Austin): can't fit both special relativity and Bell's theorem violations -> can't explain Bell tests
- Fredkin and Zuse pioneered computable universe (the former: book line on world as cellular automaton; later Fredkin's toy model Salt)
  - claim NKS takes these as its own; but Wolfram's model is a rewriting network, not CA (CA can't handle no absolute time frame)
- Jürgen Schmidhuber: Turing-machine-computable physics taken without attribution
- Weinberg 2002 review quote (lapsed particle physicist ... carpenter, moon, wood)

## Natural selection

- Wolfram: natural selection not fundamental cause of complexity in biology
- Chris Lavers: Wolfram doesn't understand evolution

## Originality

- not original/important enough for title and claims
- rule 110 Turing completeness proof by Matthew Cook, not Wolfram

Some scientists criticized the book, including Cosma Shalizi and Scott Aaronson. They saw a fatal flaw in it, which is that simple systems like cellular automata are not complex enough to describe how complex evolved systems are, and they said Wolfram ignored the research that categorizes the complexity of systems. The critics accept Wolfram's result that shows universal computation, but they think it is minor and they dispute his claim that it is a paradigm shift. Other people thought the work had valuable insights and refreshing ideas. Wolfram answered his critics in a series of blog posts.

## Scientific philosophy

So NKS argues that if you explore the space of simple programs systematically you will get a base of knowledge that can be reused. But a lot of scientists believe that out of all possible parameters only some actually occur in the universe. For example, out of all the possible permutations of the symbols that make up an equation, most will be basically meaningless. NKS has also been criticized for saying that the behavior of simple systems is somehow representative of all systems.

## Methodology

A common criticism is that NKS does not follow the established scientific methodology. For example, NKS does not give rigorous mathematical definitions and it does not try to prove theorems, and most of the formulas and equations are written in Mathematica and not in standard notation. In the same way NKS has been criticized for being very visual, with a lot of the information given in pictures that don't have formal meaning. It was also criticized for not using modern research in the field of complexity, especially work on complexity from a rigorous mathematical perspective. It was also criticized for misrepresenting chaos theory.

## Utility

NKS has been criticized for not giving specific results that can be applied right away to ongoing scientific research. There is also criticism, implicit and explicit, that studying simple programs has little connection to the physical universe and so it is of limited value. Steven Weinberg pointed out that no real-world system has been satisfactorily explained with Wolfram's methods. The mathematician Steven G. Krantz wrote, "Just because Wolfram can cook up a cellular automaton that seems to produce the spot pattern on a leopard, may we safely conclude that he understands the mechanism by which the spots are produced on the leopard, or why the spots are there, or what function (evolutionary or mating or camouflage or other) they perform?"

## Principle of computational equivalence (PCE)

The principle of computational equivalence (PCE) has been criticized for being vague and unmathematical and for not making predictions that can be verified directly. It was also criticized for going against the spirit of research in mathematical logic and computational complexity theory, which try to make fine-grained distinctions between levels of computational sophistication, and for wrongly mixing up different kinds of universality property. Also, critics like Ray Kurzweil argued that it ignores the difference between hardware and software, because even if two computers are equivalent in power, that does not mean any two programs they run are equivalent too. Other people say it is not much more than a new name for the Church–Turing thesis.

## The fundamental theory (NKS Chapter 9)

Wolfram's speculations about a direction toward a fundamental theory of physics have been criticized as being vague and obsolete. Scott Aaronson, who is Professor of Computer Science at University of Texas Austin, also claims that Wolfram's methods can't be compatible with both special relativity and Bell's theorem violations, and so they can't explain the observed results of Bell tests.

The idea of a computable universe was pioneered by Edward Fredkin and Konrad Zuse, the former by writing a line in his book about how the world might be like a cellular automaton, and Fredkin developed this further later using a toy model called Salt. Some have claimed that NKS tries to take these ideas as its own, but Wolfram's model of the universe is a rewriting network and not a cellular automaton, because Wolfram himself suggested that a cellular automaton can't account for relativistic features like there being no absolute time frame. Jürgen Schmidhuber also charged that his work on Turing machine-computable physics was stolen without attribution, namely his idea of enumerating possible Turing-computable universes.

Steven Weinberg, the Nobel laureate and elementary particle physicist, wrote in a 2002 review of NKS, "Wolfram himself is a lapsed elementary particle physicist, and I suppose he can't resist trying to apply his experience with digital computer programs to the laws of nature. This has led him to the view (also considered in a 1981 paper by Richard Feynman) that nature is discrete rather than continuous. He suggests that space consists of a set of isolated points, like cells in a cellular automaton, and that even time flows in discrete steps. Following an idea of Edward Fredkin, he concludes that the universe itself would then be an automaton, like a giant computer. It's possible, but I can't see any motivation for these speculations, except that this is the sort of system that Wolfram and others have become used to in their work on computers. So might a carpenter, looking at the moon, suppose that it is made of wood."

## Natural selection

Wolfram claimed that natural selection is not the fundamental cause of complexity in biology, and this led the journalist Chris Lavers to say that Wolfram does not understand the theory of evolution.

## Originality

NKS has been criticized as not being original or important enough to justify its title and its claims.

The book presents a huge number of examples and arguments in an authoritative way, and this has been criticized because it leads the reader to believe that each of them is Wolfram's own. In particular, one of the most substantial new technical results in the book, that the rule 110 cellular automaton is Turing complete, was not proven by Wolfram. Wolfram credits the proof to Matthew Cook, his research assistant.

Although critics accept Wolfram's result showing universal computation, they view it as minor and dispute his claim of a paradigm shift. Others found valuable insights and refreshing ideas in the work.[6,7] Wolfram addressed his critics in a series of blog posts.[8,9]

## Scientific philosophy

A tenet of NKS is that the simpler the system, the more likely a version of it will recur in a wide variety of more complicated contexts. NKS therefore argues that systematically exploring the space of simple programs will lead to a base of reusable knowledge. But many scientists believe that of all possible parameters, only some actually occur in the universe; of all possible permutations of the symbols making up an equation, for instance, most will be essentially meaningless. NKS has also been criticized for asserting that the behavior of simple systems is somehow representative of all systems.

## Methodology

A common criticism of NKS is that it does not follow established scientific methodology. NKS does not establish rigorous mathematical definitions,[10] for instance, nor does it attempt to prove theorems, and most of its formulas and equations are written in Mathematica rather than in standard notation.[11] Along these lines, NKS has been criticized for being heavily visual, conveying much information through pictures that lack formal meaning.[7] It has also been criticized for not using modern research in the field of complexity, particularly work on complexity from a rigorous mathematical perspective, and for misrepresenting chaos theory.

## Utility

NKS has been criticized for not providing specific results that are immediately applicable to ongoing scientific research.[7] There has also been criticism, implicit and explicit, that the study of simple programs has little connection to the physical universe and is therefore of limited value. ## Principle of computational equivalence (PCE)

The principle of computational equivalence (PCE) has been criticized for being vague and unmathematical, and for not making directly verifiable predictions.[11] It has also been criticized for being contrary to the spirit of research in mathematical logic and computational complexity theory, which seek to make fine-grained distinctions between levels of computational sophistication, and for wrongly conflating different kinds of universality property.[11] Critics such as Ray Kurzweil have also argued that it ignores the distinction between hardware and software: two computers may be equivalent in power, but it does not follow that any two programs they might run are also equivalent.[14] Others suggest it is little more than a rechristening of the Church–Turing thesis.

## The fundamental theory (NKS Chapter 9)

Wolfram's speculations on a direction toward a fundamental theory of physics have been criticized as vague and obsolete. Scott Aaronson, Professor of Computer Science at University of Texas Austin, also claims that Wolfram's methods cannot be compatible with both special relativity and Bell's theorem violations, and therefore cannot explain the observed results of Bell tests.[15]

Edward Fredkin and Konrad Zuse pioneered the idea of a computable universe, the former by writing a line in his book on how the world might be like a cellular automaton, later developed further by Fredkin using a toy model called Salt.[16] It has been claimed that NKS tries to take these ideas as its own, but Wolfram's model of the universe is a rewriting network, not a cellular automaton, since Wolfram himself has suggested that a cellular automaton cannot account for relativistic features such as the absence of an absolute time frame.[17] Jürgen Schmidhuber has also charged that his work on Turing machine-computable physics, namely his idea of enumerating possible Turing-computable universes, was stolen without attribution.[18]

In a 2002 review of NKS, the Nobel laureate and elementary particle physicist Steven Weinberg wrote, "Wolfram himself is a lapsed elementary particle physicist, and I suppose he can't resist trying to apply his experience with digital computer programs to the laws of nature. This has led him to the view (also considered in a 1981 paper by Richard Feynman) that nature is discrete rather than continuous. He suggests that space consists of a set of isolated points, like cells in a cellular automaton, and that even time flows in discrete steps. Following an idea of Edward Fredkin, he concludes that the universe itself would then be an automaton, like a giant computer. It's possible, but I can't see any motivation for these speculations, except that this is the sort of system that Wolfram and others have become used to in their work on computers. So might a carpenter, looking at the moon, suppose that it is made of wood."[19]

## Natural selection

Wolfram's claim that natural selection is not the fundamental cause of complexity in biology led journalist Chris Lavers to say that Wolfram does not understand the theory of evolution.[20]

## Originality

NKS has been criticized as not original or important enough to justify its title and claims.

The authoritative way in which NKS presents a vast number of examples and arguments has been criticized as leading readers to believe that each of them is original to Wolfram. In particular, one of the most substantial new technical results in the book, that the rule 110 cellular automaton is Turing complete, was not proven by Wolfram, who credits the proof to his research assistant Matthew Cook.[21]
